title: Tested steady discs permit a 13-orbit ASASSN-14ko drag stall only at inclinations up to 15 degrees
abstract: We test a precessing star-disc drag clock for ASASSN-14ko. We close the relation between the 108.44-day period, mass, eccentricity and the earlier fitted precession rates. We solve a steady alpha disc over both crossing radii. We define a weak-drag interval by absolute orbital energy loss below 20 percent of its full-cycle positive maximum. In a grid with log mass 7.00-7.90, log luminosity 44.50-45.30, alpha 0.01-0.1 and inclination 5-60 degrees, a 13-orbit interval occurs only through 15 degrees after a stated thin-crossing screen. At 25-60 degrees the maximum is 9.52 orbits. A seven-orbit interval permits 33 degrees. These are conditional grid results, not confidence limits or an inclination measurement. Eccentricity 0.85 at the earlier precession rates fixes log mass to 7.084-7.145; it cannot be assigned unchanged to a higher mass. We also fit 22 published X-ray and optical half-rise times. A frozen-element clock at 25 degrees fits the eight X-ray times with chi-square 2.57 while its period spans 107.80-108.88 days during cycles 20-33. Thus a straight sampled clock need not imply near-zero drag at each passage. A normalization audit shows a strong dependence on disc viscosity. A torque audit gives a 5.6 percent change of the semi-latus rectum across the record for this example, so it is not a coupled dynamical solution. No new observation or unique physical clock is claimed. Code, input hashes, synthetic grids, aggregate fits and figures are included; source timing records remain external.

display.caption: Orbit closure and weak-drag duration in the tested steady discs. The 13-orbit bound is conditional on a specified energy-loss threshold, grid and thin-crossing screen. It is not an inclination measurement.

Maximum duration below 20 percent of the full-phase positive orbital energy loss. The map maximizes over tested disc and precession parameters. The contours mark seven and 13 orbits. This is a feasibility map, not a probability map.

Synthetic predictions of a selected 25-degree frozen-element clock. Small residuals at the eight sampled X-ray cycle positions can hide a changing period and torque. Dots are model values, not observations. The torque audit shows why this curve is not a self-consistent dynamical solution.
